blocks.html: The World Wide Web (WWW) is a huge collection of linked documents and resources that can be accessed over the internet using a web browser. It was invented by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in 1989; the first website went online in 1991.
The internet is the network of networks (the roads). The web is one service that runs on it (the vehicles). Email, video calls and online games are other services on the same internet.

rows: A single document on the web, written in HTML
A collection of related web pages under one domain name
The main or first page of a website
Text or an image that takes you to another page when clicked
A computer that stores websites and sends pages to browsers on request
Software that requests, receives and displays web pages: Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari
The address of a resource, e.g.https://www.example.com/class10/results.htm l
Content changes for each user or over time
Stored as a ready HTML file
Created by programs on the server when requested, often using a database
Example: board result page showing your marks, a cricket live score

items.html: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) — the structure and content of a page.
CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) — colours, fonts and layout.
JavaScript — interactivity in the browser (menus, form checks, animations).
Server-side languages — such as PHP, Java, Python and C# — build dynamic pages on the server.
Databases — such as MySQL — store the data behind dynamic sites.

lessons.title: 12.3 Domain names, hosting and search engines

items.html: A domain name (e.g. myschool.in ) is bought from a domain registrar for a yearly fee. The .in domain is managed in India by NIXI; government sites use .gov.in .
Web hosting means renting space on an always-on web server so the website is available 24 × 7.
The domain is pointed to the hosting server through DNS.
Crawling — automated programs called crawlers (spiders, bots) visit pages and follow links.
Indexing — the words and information of each page are stored in a huge index, like the index at the back of this book.
Ranking — when you search, the engine looks up its index and orders the results by relevance, quality and other signals.

rows: "Read-only" web: static pages created by a few publishers
"Read-write" social web: users create and share content
Blogs, wikis, social media, video sharing, reviews
"Read-write-own": a smarter, more personalised and decentralised web using AI and blockchain ideas

items.html: Blog — an online diary or article site, with posts shown newest first.
Wiki — a website that many users can edit together, e.g. an online encyclopedia.
Social networking — sharing posts, photos and messages with friends and followers.
Forums — discussion boards on topics.
Video sharing and streaming, e-learning portals, online maps, cloud storage.

blocks.html: Electronic mail (email) is a method of sending messages and files from one person to another over the internet. The first network email between two computers was sent by Ray Tomlinson in 1971; he chose the @ symbol to separate the user from the computer name.
riya.kumari@schoolmail.in

items.html: Username (riya.kumari ) — unique on that mail service.
@ — means "at".
Domain name (schoolmail.in ) — the mail service provider or organisation.

blocks.html: Rules: no spaces; letters, digits, dots, hyphens and underscores are usually allowed; email addresses are not case-sensitive in practice.

blocks.caption: Figure 12.1 · How an email travels from sender to receiver

rows: Sends mail from your app to your mail server and from server to server
Downloads mail to one device and usually removes it from the server
Keeps mail on the server and keeps all your devices in sync — used by most webmail and phone apps

blocks.html: Webmail is used through a browser (e.g. any popular free mail website). An email client is an installed app, such as Microsoft Outlook or Mozilla Thunderbird, or the mail app on a phone.

lessons.title: 12.6 Parts and features of an email

rows: Others who should know; all receivers can see these addresses
Hidden receivers — use when mailing many people so that their addresses stay private
A short, clear title, e.g. "Leave application – Riya Kumari, Class 10-A"
Files sent with the mail; most services limit size to about 20–25 MB — share larger files as a cloud link
Automatic closing with name, class/designation and contact
Answer the sender and everyone in To and CC
Send the received mail to someone new

items.html: Inbox — received mail; Sent — mail you sent; Drafts — unfinished mail; Spam / Junk — unwanted or suspicious mail; Trash / Bin — deleted mail (emptied after some days); Starred / Important — marked mail.
Labels or folders to group mail; filters (rules) to sort incoming mail automatically; search to find old mail; auto-reply (out of office); scheduled send; undo send.
Use a clear subject and a polite greeting ("Respected Sir/Madam", "Dear Riya").
Keep the message short and to the point; check spelling.
Do not write in ALL CAPITALS.
Use BCC for group mails; do not use Reply All unnecessarily.
Mention attachments in the body and check that they are attached.
Reply within a reasonable time.
Spam is unwanted bulk mail; do not reply to it or click its links.
Be careful with phishing mail that imitates banks, schools or delivery companies.
Do not open unexpected attachments, especially .exe , .zip or macro-enabled files.
Use a strong password and two-step verification.
Log out on shared computers.

blocks.html: Did you know? More than 300 billion emails are sent every day worldwide — and a large share of them is spam caught by automatic filters.

The WWW is a collection of linked web pages on the internet, invented by Tim Berners-Lee; browsers request pages from web servers using URLs.
Static pages are the same for everyone; dynamic pages are built for each request using server programs and databases.
HTML gives structure, CSS gives style and JavaScript gives interactivity.
Websites need a domain name and web hosting; search engines crawl, index and rank pages.
Web 1.0 was read-only, Web 2.0 is social and user-created, Web 3.0 is emerging.
Email addresses have a username, @ and a domain. SMTP sends mail; POP3 and IMAP retrieve it.
Email parts: From, To, CC, BCC, Subject, Body, Attachment and Signature; folders and filters organise mail.
Follow email etiquette and watch out for spam and phishing.
